div.p: Geographically weighted regression (GWR) is a classic and widely used approach to model spatial non-stationarity. However, the approach makes no precise expressions of its weighting kernels and is insufficient to estimate complex geographical processes. To resolve these problems, we proposed a geographically neural network weighted regression (GNNWR) model that combines ordinary least squares (OLS) and neural networks to estimate spatial nonstationarity based on a concept similar to GWR. Specifically, we designed a spatially weighted neural network (SWNN) to represent the nonstationary weight matrix in GNNWR and developed two case studies to examine the effectiveness of GNNWR. The first case used simulated datasets, and the second case, environmental observations from the coastal areas of Zhejiang. The results showed that GNNWR achieved better fitting accuracy and more adequate prediction than OLS and GWR. In addition, GNNWR is applicable to addressing spatial non-stationarity in various domains with complex geographical processes.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The geographically weighted regression (GWR) model proposed by Brunsdon et al. (1996), is a geostatistical technique that takes spatial non-stationarity into account by permitting the relationship between independent variables and dependent variables to change locally. The GWR model is proven effective to estimate spatial non-stationarity and has attracted significant attention in the past few decades. The GWR model and its expanded models are widely applied in diverse fields, including housing price analysis (Huang et al. 2010, Wu et al. 2014, Fotheringham et al. 2015a, 2015b, Yao and Fotheringham 2016), wildfire analysis (Rodrigues et al. 2014), PM 2.5 estimation (Ma et al. 2014), urban surface heat prediction (Su et al. 2012), disease analysis (Nakaya et al. 2005), forest ecosystem analysis (Wang et al. 2005), and land-use modelling (Tu 2011).

The key component of the GWR model is a spatial weight matrix, which represents local spatial relationships. In general, spatial weights are calculated based on chosen spatial kernel functions in which closer samples are assigned larger weights. Therefore, the choice of spatial kernels is crucial to the GWR model. Currently, the two most common weighting mechanisms are the fixed kernel and the adaptive kernel. In the fixed kernel, the distance (bandwidth) remains constant while the count of selected neighbours (q value) varies accordingly. In the adaptive kernel, the bandwidth varies while q value remains the same. Gaussian-based kernels, the bi-square kernel and the tri-cube kernel (Fotheringham et al. 1998(Fotheringham et al. , 2002) ) are three typical kernel functions in the two abovementioned weighting mechanisms.

Although GWR provides great support in the analysis and prediction of spatial nonstationarity, the method is difficult to model complex geographical processes in three reasons. Firstly, GWR often fails to accurately estimate non-stationarity due to the difficulty in choosing the right kernel function for complex relationships. Secondly, the form of the weighting function requires a priori assumptions, although more flexible functions can be used in theory. Thirdly, the kernel equation is often relatively simple but unable to address complicated nonlinear interactions inherent in the geographic phenomena.

In fact, the calculation of the weight matrix can be considered as a complicated nonlinear problem between spatial distances and spatial weights. Recently, neural networks have been widely used to solve nonlinear problems owing to their excellent fitting abilities across fields such as geological disaster prediction (Wang et al. 2016, Lee et al. 2017), meteorological environmental modelling (Montazerolghaem et al. 2016, Li et al. 2017), behavioural trajectory analysis (Alahi et al. 2016, Al-Molegi et al. 2016), and marine disaster prediction (Qin et al. 2017, Du et al. 2018a, 2018b). To compensate for the abovementioned deficiencies of the GWR model, we introduced here a neural network model to estimate the complicated nonlinear effects of nonstationary relationships. Based on a concept similar to the GWR model, we proposed a geographically neural network weighted regression (GNNWR) model that combines ordinary least squares (OLS) and a neural network for the accurate estimation of the spatial non-stationarity. GNNWR uses a spatial weighted neural network (SWNN) to calculate nonstationary weights.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the GNNWR model, followed by the definition of SWNN and the process of integrating SWNN with OLS to develop the GNNWR model. Section 3 contains experiments and comparisons of the OLS, GWR and GNNWR models for two case studies. The conclusions are given in the last section.

div.head: GWR model
div.p: The basic concern associated with the GWR model is that a global model's coefficient estimates may be unable to express the sophisticated local variations over space. Therefore, the global form is extended by the GWR to allow local estimations, and the GWR can be mathematically expressed as (Fotheringham et al. 2002):
div.formula: y i ¼ β 0 u i ; v i ð Þþ X p k¼1 β k u i ; v i ð Þx ik þ ε i i ¼ 1; 2; Á Á Á ; n(4)
div.p: where u i ; v i ð Þ represents the coordinates of pointi in space and
div.formula: β 0 u i ; v i ð Þ denotes the intercept value. β k u i ; v i ð Þ is a series of coefficient values at the point i.
div.p: In the GWR model, by allowing the coefficient values to vary spatially, one can capture the local effects. The estimation of the coefficient values β u i ; v i ð Þcan be expressed as (Fotheringham et al. 2002):
div.formula: β u i ; v i ð Þ¼ X T W u i ; v i ð ÞX Â Ã À1 X T W u i ; v i ð Þy(5)

A certain weight kernel is used to calculate the weight matrix for each pointi. In the GWR model, the weight kernels usually adopted are the Gaussian, bi-square, tri-cube and exponential functions and can be either fixed or adaptive. For instance, the fixed Gaussian-based kernel function can be expressed as (Fotheringham et al. 2002):

div.p: where b, the bandwidth, is a non-negative attenuation parameter that produces a declining effect relative to the distance d s ij . Adaptive kernels, which use adaptive bandwidths, are commonly constructed to ensure adequate local calibration when the samples are dense or sparse. For instance, the form of an adaptive bi-square weighting function is as follows (Fotheringham et al. 2002):

div.p: where b i denotes the distance from a point i to its qth nearest neighbour, and thus, the estimation of the adaptive kernel is equal to the calibration of the q value (Fotheringham et al. 2002).

div.head: Model diagnosis
div.p: Testing for spatial non-stationarity of the parameters in the GNNWR model is quite important and some appropriate statistics for model diagnosis should be developed. The optimal bandwidth of the weight kernel should be determined prior to computing the final weighting matrix of GWR model. Its optimization procedure is commonly based on cross-validation or AICc values with the y values. Similar to GWR, the optimal parameters in the SWNN of GNNWR are also related to the observations, and, therefore, the exact distributions of the testing statistics for these local models are difficult to determine. Alternatively, as Leung et al. (2000) have suggested, using approximated distributions is a feasible way to solve the model testing problem from a practical perspective. div.head: Model design and estimation
div.p: The estimation process of the GNNWR model is shown in Figure 2. First, we randomly divide the data into three sets: training dataset, validation dataset and testing dataset. It should be noted that the OLS coefficients, which denote the average relationship, are calculated from the training dataset.

In the modelling procedure, the distances from the estimated point p i of the three datasets (training, validation, and testing) to all training points are computed as the input layer for the SWNN. Through the calculations of the SWNN, the output layer derives the nonstationary weights of p i , and each weight corresponds to one independent variable as predefined. Therefore, the nonstationary coefficients are obtained by multiplying the nonstationary weights with the pre-calculated OLS coefficients. Accordingly, the fitted value ŷi is the result of summing the multiplications of all the nonstationary coefficients and their corresponding independent variables.

The training dataset is used to optimize the network weights and biases of the SWNN, and the validation dataset is used to determine whether the model is overfitted after each training epoch. After training completion, we use the testing dataset to evaluate the model's generalization and prediction capacities through a similar process of validation. Noteworthily, the validation and testing datasets do not participate in the OLS estimation and model training. In addition, the GNNWR model is able to obtain the spatial nonstationary coefficients for any point.

The proposed neural network architectures and training strategy of the GNNWR model improve the efficiency of optimization processes. The neural network adopts a fully connected layer and dropout technologies to enhance the generalization capability, as suggested by Srivastava et al. (2014). In addition, we use the parameter initialization method and activation function developed by He et al. (2015) in each hidden layer to improve the optimization efficiency. Moreover, we adopt the batch normalization technique proposed by Ioffe and Szegedy (2015) to reduce the influence of the internal covariate transformation problem so that the model can set a larger learning rate and further enhance the computing power of the GNNWR model.

div.head: Model training and validation
div.p: We use the mini-batch stochastic gradient descent algorithm for model training. The mean square error (MSE) serves the training loss function for the GNNWR model. The MSE value of the validation dataset is used as the overfitting criterion. If the overfitting indicator shows a continuous rise or flat trend and exceeds a predefined tolerance count, the model is considered to be overfitted, and the training will stop. The training and validation procedures of the GNNWR model are shown in Figure 3.
Step 1: Disorder the training dataset automatically and initialize the network parameters of the GNNWR model, such as the maximal iterations, number of neurons, learning rate, bath size, and so on.

Step 2: Obtain the first or next mini-batch of data from the training dataset. Step 4: Conduct the early stop strategy and check the number of training iterations. In the early stop method, we use the MSE value of the validation dataset to judge the model overfitting. During the training process, the best validation accuracy and model parameters are recorded. When the MSE value of the validation dataset does not descend for a predefined tolerance count of consecutive epochs, the model is considered overfitted, and the training process will stop. Then, the latest recorded best model will be restored as the final model. In addition, if the maximum number of training iterations is reached, we also stop the training process. Otherwise, we disorder the training dataset and update the epoch number. Then, repeat Step 2.
The pseudocode implementation of the GNNWR model is attached as Appendix A. The GNNWR model is implemented using TensorFlow 1.5.0 and Python 3.6 (see Table 1).

div.head: Evaluation method
div.p: The performance of the models is evaluated using the following criteria: the determination coefficient (R 2 ), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc). The formula of each evaluation criterion is as follows:

R 2 is a statistical criterion that reflects the fitting degree between the actual and predicted values, and the RMSE, MAE and MAPE reflect the prediction accuracy such that a smaller value of these indicators corresponds to a better predictive performance of the model.

div.head: Results and discussion
div.p: We examine the performance of the GNNWR approach in two case studies (Figure 4). We compare three different models, i.e. the global OLS, GWR and GNNWR models with the same dataset. For the GWR model, two kernel types (fixed and adaptive) and two functions (Gaussian and bi-square) are considered in the experiments. The AICc value is used as the performance criterion of the GWR model.

In case one, a simulation process is designed and repeated for 100 realizations of simulated data to comprehensively compare the GNNWR model with the OLS model and GWR models with four kernel types (Table 2). In case two, the comparison is based on an environmental modelling dataset. Due to the non-uniform distribution of the environmental dataset in space, the discontinuous weight of the fixed bi-square kernel probably leads to instability in the modelling results (Nakaya 2014). Therefore, this function is removed, and the other three kernels are utilized for comparison in the experiment with environmental observations. The GWR models are implemented using GWR4 software.

div.head: Case one: simulated dataset
div.p: We simulate datasets with known nonstationary properties and then evaluate predictions according to these data. The simulation approach follows the methods used in Harris et al. (2010) and is repeated for 100 realizations of simulated data to fully investigate the robustness of the GNNWR results.

div.head: Experimental implementation
div.p: A four-layer feed-forward network is one of the most commonly used neural network architectures and is considered to be highly effective for nonlinear problems (Tamura andTateishi 1997, Cetin et al. 2004). Therefore, we design a four-layer SWNN architecture that includes one input layer, one output layer, and two hidden layers. There is no well recognized method to determining the optimal sizes of the neurons in the hidden layers Instead, we use a simple search strategy. The optimal neuron size of the first hidden layer is selected from the list of [32,64,128,256], and the neuron size of the second hidden layer is optimized from the list of [4,8,16,32]. Therefore, 16 models are developed and compared using two statistical measures, R 2 and RMSE. The optimum neural network structures and hyper-parameters of the GNNWR model are shown in Table 3.

Figure 5 shows the performance variation of the GNNWR model. The AICc value of the GNNWR model (Figure 5(b)) for the training dataset shows a downward trend, indicating that the fitting of the model continues to increase for the training dataset. However, the MSE value of the validation dataset (Figure 5(a)) continues to rise or persists after 3,297 epochs for more than 1,500 consecutive iterations, which demonstrates that the GNNWR model is overfitted. Therefore, the optimal GNNWR model is achieved at epoch = 3,297.

In addition, although the computational complexity of GNNWR model is considerable higher than GWR model, the optimal GNNWR model can usually be achieved within several minutes with the powerful parallel computing ability of the GPU units. Moreover, the model complexity of GNNWR does not increase significantly with the rapid growth of data size, so its computational efficiency remains acceptable with big data.

div.head: Results and discussion
div.p: Table 4 shows the mean fitting results of the OLS, GWR, and GNNWR models for the training datasets of 100 simulations. The GWR and GNNWR models perform much better than the OLS model for all statistical indicators.

Comparing the results of the four GWR models shows that the GWR-AFB models are better than the GWR-AAB, GWR-AFG and GWR-AAG models according to the R 2 , RMSE, MAE, MAPE and AICc values. From Table 4, it can also be noted that the GNNWR model obtains the best performance among all the models. Comparing the results of the GNNWR and GWR models, the variance interpretation proportion has increased from 92.74% in the GWR-AFB model to 94.13% in the GNNWR model. The RMSE, MAE, MAPE value of the GWR-AFB model decreased from 0.4184 to 0.3980, 0.3264 to 0.3093, 19.98% to 18.61% of the GNNWR model. Moreover, the AICc value of the GWR-AFB model decreased from 675.655 to 437.878 in the GNNWR model.

In addition to the fitting assessment of the training dataset, the prediction performance of the testing dataset is another important measurement in a model evaluation. The performance differences between the models on the testing dataset show similar results as shown in Table 4. More specifically, since the OLS model takes no account of spatial non-stationarity, it performs the worst among all the models. In addition, all statistical indicators of the GNNWR model are superior to those of the four GWR models, which indicates that the GNNWR model achieves a better prediction accuracy than the other models.

Figures 6 and 7 compare the model estimations with the simulated dataset to assess whether the GNNWR and GWR models capture the nonstationary features of spatial relationships. Figure 6(a-d) displays the values of y,

div.p: for the GNNWR model are more precise and more similar to the stimulated images than those of the four GWR models. For example, with regard to the image of β 0 u i ; v i ð Þ, its middle area is similar to a diamond with high values, and the corner values are lower than the middle area. A comparison of Figure 6(f,j, n,r,v) shows that the GNNWR model achieves a better prediction ability, and its predicted image is closer to the simulated image than that of the GWR models. Moreover, the GNNWR model estimate the values of the four corners well compared to the other models.

Figure 7 shows similar conclusions in examining the mean parameter estimates of GWR and GNNWR models over 100 simulated datasets. This finding demonstrates that the ability of GNNWR to replicate the local processes is remarkably robust. In addition, the boxplots of RMSE and Pearson's r between the estimated values and the real values over 100 simulated datasets in Figure 8 further confirms the superiority of GNNWR model to GWR models. The RMSE and Pearson's r of the GNNWR model are considerably better than the four GWR models, which also provides additional evidence on the robustness of GNNWR model. In summary, by using the superior learning ability of the neural network, the GNNWR model efficiently captures the non-stationary characteristics of the relationships, and exactly constructs the nonstationary weight matrix and spatially varying coefficients.

div.head: Study area and data
div.p: The second case study is in the coastal area of Zhejiang (CAZ), China (Figure 4(b)). Red tides is the primary cause of marine ecological damage in the CAZ and causes serious harm to the economic development and public safety in Zhejiang Province (Zhang et al. 2017). Exploring the interactions between the various environmental factors is important for red tide monitoring. Many studies show that the red tide process is significantly associated with marine physical, chemical and biological factors (Qin et al. 2017, Du et al. 2018a, 2018b). We use the GNNWR model to investigate the spatially nonstationary relationships between red tide indicators and a set of environmental variables to better reveal the environmental factors to red tide disasters in the CAZ.

The experimental dataset was collected by the Marine Monitoring and Forecasting Center of Zhejiang Province (Hangzhou, China). Because the springtime is the traditional period for red tide outbreaks in the CAZ, the water quality data collected in the spring of 2016 are selected as the experimental data. The data include five water quality variables, including the dissolved oxygen (DO), salinity (SAL), phosphate (PO 4 ), inorganic nitrogen (IN) and Chl-a. The Chl-a concentration is selected as the dependent variable since it is usually considered the main measure of phytoplankton biomass and is utilized to assess the red tides (Du et al. 2018b). The DO and SAL are significantly correlated with the Chl-a concentration through a correctional analysis, and the variance inflation factor (VIF) values also indicate that the multicollinearity among them are comparatively low (Table 5). Therefore, DO and SAL are selected as the independent variables in this study.

The total dataset contains 311 records and is randomly divided into three parts: a training dataset (235 observations), a validation dataset (50 observations), and a test dataset (26 observations) (Figure 4(b), Table 6). The range of the Chl-a concentration is 0.600 ~70.100 ug/L, and the average value is 23.327 ug/L (Table 6). Because the extent of each variable is quite different, all factors are normalized into the [0, 1] range for modelling.

div.head: Experimental implementation
div.p: The implementation details are similar to those of the simulated dataset. Table 7 shows the optimal neural network structures and hyper-parameter settings of the GNNWR model.

div.head: Results and discussion
div.p: The global OLS model is implemented as the base model and is used to study the average relationships between the Chl-a concentration and the selected variables (Table 8). According to the p-value of the t-test, the DO variable is significant at the level of 0.001. In addition, the SAL and DO variables are both positively associated with the Chl-a concentration. The results of the GNNWR model and three GWR models (i.e. the GWR-AFG, GWR-AAB, and GWR-AAG models) are shown in Table 9. The GWR and GNNWR models are both considerably better than the OLS model for all statistical indicators. The F 1 testing results of the GWR and GNNWR models further demonstrate that the relationships between the explanatory variables and the Chl-a concentration are significantly nonstationary across space. Comparing the results of the three GWR models, we find that the GWR-AFG model obtains the best fitness performance according to the R 2 and RMSE values (0.6726 and 6.0018, respectively), which are considerably better than those of the GWR-AAB (0.6319 and 6.3905, respectively) and the GWR-AAG (0.6350 and 6.3725, respectively) models.

In addition, the R 2 , RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and AICc values of the GNNWR model are substantially better than those of three GWR models. Notably, the value of R 2 increased from 0.6726 in the GWR-AFG model to 0.8552 in the GNNWR model. Moreover, the RMSE and AICc values in the GWR-AFG model decreased from 6.0018 and 462.162 to 3.9956 and 354.896, respectively, in the GNNWR model. As shown in Figure 9, the three GWR models have a relatively high precision for fitting low values but are unable to estimate high values. For the GNNWR model, the estimates of both low and high values are close to the real values, which is much better than the GWR models, especially for the high values. Therefore, the GNNWR model greatly improves the fitting performance for cases with spatial non-stationarity and is obviously superior to the classical GWR model in this experiment.

Table 9 also shows the prediction results of the OLS, GWR and GNNWR models for the test dataset. The predictive ability of the OLS model is still the worst of all the models. Comparing the prediction results of three GWR models, we can observe that the GWR-AAG model obtains the best prediction performance, although the GWR-AFG model performs best for the training dataset, which indicates that the GWR-AFG model is probably overfitted. The statistical indicators for the GNNWR model for the testing dataset are substantially better than those of the GWR models. For example, the RMSE and MAPE values of the GWR-AAG model decreased from 5.2021% and 58.51% to 3.7607% and 49.48%, respectively, of the GNNWR model, and the R 2 increased from 0.7525 to 0.8466. Obviously, the GNNWR model efficiently captures the non-stationary characteristics of the relationships and obtains an excellent generalization performance compared to the OLS and GWR methods.

div.head: Spatial non-stationarity of variables.
div.p: The F 1 test of the GNNWR and GWR models in Table 9 shows that the relationships between the Chl-a concentration and the DO and SAL variables have significant non-stationary features in the whole. To further explore whether each set of variables varies notably in space, F 2 tests are performed on the coefficients of each independent variable for the GWR and GNNWR models (Table 10). From the F 2 test results of the GWR and GNNWR models, we can see that the significance level of each variable reaches 0.001. Therefore, the estimated relationships not only have significant spatial non-stationarity overall but also show clear non-stationarity features for each independent variable. Similar to the GWR model, we can further analyse the distribution of the GNNWR model coefficients to explore their variability as displayed in Table 11. The variable coefficients of the GWR and GNNWR models contain both positive and negative values, suggesting that the influences of the water quality variables on the Chl-a concentration may show opposite effects in different locations due to the influence of spatial non-stationarity.

There is substantial spatial variation in the GNNWR model's local estimates (Figure 10), indicating that the spatial effects changeover space with strong non-stationarity. The DO variable exhibits strong positive effects on the Chl-a concentration in the northern area of the CAZ, with these positive effects gradually diminishing from north to south. The SAL variable shows weak negative effects on the Chl-a concentration in the economically developed areas of the Zhejiang Province, such as Hangzhou Bay, Ningbo, Taizhou and Wenzhou but shows much greater negative effects when far away from the coastal areas.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this study, based on a concept similar to the GWR model, we propose a GNNWR model that combines OLS with an SWNN model to estimate spatial non-stationarity. SWNN is designed to precisely construct the nonstationary weight matrix by using the superior fitting ability of the neural network model. Similar to the GWR model, the GNNWR model can be used to address spatial non-stationarity in various social events, environmental processes and human activities.

Case studies on both simulated and real environmental datasets indicate that the GNNWR model achieved better fitting and prediction performances than the OLS and GWR models. For the results of the fitting performance comparison among the OLS, GWR and GNNWR models, the R 2 of the GNNWR model is better than that of the OLS and GWR models, and the statistical indicators, namely, the RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and AICc, also show the substantial improvements. Moreover, the GNNWR model can better capture the nonstationary characteristics of the relationships and obtain a better generalization performance than the other models due to the learning ability of neural network. Consequently, we conclude that the GNNWR model not only significantly improves the fitting performance for spatial non-stationarity but also obtains the strongest prediction performance. Furthermore, we also demonstrate that the SWNN is powerful and meaningful.

Although the GNNWR model has excellent modelling capability, its computational efficiency is not as good as the GWR model. Therefore, GNNWR is more appropriate for complicated spatial relationship modelling, but for simple and fast estimations, GWR is a better choice.

In the future, more experiments should be conducted in different fields to further investigate the applicability of the GNNWR model and to explore the significant test method for the GNNWR coefficients. Furthermore, the effects of spatial autocorrelation and anisotropy should be considered and incorporated into the GNNWR model to handle even more complicated spatial relationships.
